Since China's first crewed flight in 2003, only Chinese astronauts have flown Shenzhou. Shenzhou-24 changes that: a Pakistani payload specialist will join two Chinese crewmates on the Tiangong space station for about a week. He will run four experiments picked from over 300 proposals. One Shenzhou-23 astronaut stays aboard for China's first year-long stay, freeing a seat home.

Reality check: the rocket is on the pad, but China has not announced a launch date.

[TODAY] Almost 7 hours outside for 55 more kilowatts. 🔋

On Nov. 5, NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk spent 6 hours, 59 minutes outside the International Space Station. They installed and unrolled the eighth and final new roll-out solar array.

The upgrade lifts the station's power capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215. The project began in February 2021 and took 18 spacewalks.

Reality check: the work is done, but the new arrays now have to keep delivering for the rest of the station's life.

Could you handle a seven-hour spacewalk? Tell us below.

[TODAY] Why does Tuesday's full Moon look bigger? 🌕

The Moon's orbit is not a circle. Each month it swings between about 363,300 km and 405,500 km from Earth. When a full Moon lands near the close end, we call it a supermoon. Tuesday, Nov. 24, is one, the first of three in a row through January.

At most, a supermoon looks 14% bigger and 30% brighter than the year's faintest full Moon. It can also nudge tides a little higher.

Reality check: by eye the difference is subtle. A Moon low on the horizon looks huge because of the Moon illusion, which happens with every full Moon.

Save this and look east around sunset on Tuesday.

[TODAY] 28 light-years away, a trio that shouldn't exist. ⭐

Astronomers hunting for planets saw a small red star wobble far too much. The culprit was a hidden white dwarf, the dense core of a dead star, circling it every 9.8 years. A second white dwarf orbits farther out. The system, Welopō‘ai, sits 27.6 light-years away: the closest known trio with more than one white dwarf.

The puzzle: before it died, the inner white dwarf's star should have swollen into a giant that nearly swallowed its red partner. The partner survived on a wide orbit.

Reality check: how it escaped is unclear; the outer white dwarf may have helped.

Lucky escape or a helping hand? Tell us below.

[IMAGINE] Laser-fused fake Moon dust became snap-together bricks. 🧱

What is real: University of Arkansas engineers fused a powder that mimics Apollo-era Moon soil, layer by layer, with a laser. The blocks, a few centimeters wide and shaped like crosses and H's, fit together like toy bricks. No binder was added, so nothing extra would need to fly from Earth.

Reality check: the blocks are more porous and weaker than versions made with binders. They stand on their own but cannot carry loads yet. Tests in vacuum and low gravity are still needed.

The speculation: what if a Moon base were built from the very ground it stands on?

What would you build first on the Moon? Tell us below.
